title: The Tyranny of Metrics (עריצות המדדים)
text: There is a seductive comfort in numbers. A metric promises objectivity, a clean verdict untouched by human bias. Yet what we choose to measure inevitably shapes what we come to value, and the unmeasurable — kindness, originality, depth — quietly slips from view. The danger is not measurement itself, but our willingness to mistake the measurable for the meaningful.

glossary.definition: מפתה — מושך באופן שקשה לעמוד בפניו

questions.question: What does the writer warn against?
options: Mistaking the measurable for the meaningful

title: On Boredom (על השעמום)
text: We have grown so adept at banishing boredom that we have forgotten what it was for. Those empty, restless moments once nudged the mind toward daydream and invention; now they are filled instantly with a glowing screen. Perhaps creativity was never the enemy of idleness but its quiet offspring, and in eliminating one we have unwittingly starved the other.

Creativity is called…

title: The Paradox of Choice (פרדוקס הבחירה)
text: We assume that more options make us freer and happier, yet beyond a point the opposite holds. Faced with dozens of nearly identical choices, we grow anxious, postpone deciding, and feel less satisfied with whatever we finally pick. Abundance, it turns out, can be its own kind of burden, and the freedom to choose can quietly curdle into the fear of choosing wrongly.

questions.question: What is the paradox described?
options: More options can make us less happy

title: The Ship of Theseus (ספינת תזאוס)
text: If every plank of a ship is gradually replaced, is it still the same ship? The ancient puzzle endures because it quietly applies to us. Our cells, opinions and memories are continually swapped out, and yet we cling to a sense of a single, continuous self. Identity, perhaps, is less a fixed object than a story we keep telling about change.

questions.question: What does the puzzle ultimately apply to, per the text?
How does the writer redefine identity?
options: A story we tell about change
questions.explanation: 'a story we keep telling about change'.

title: Against Nostalgia (נגד הנוסטלגיה)
text: Nostalgia flatters the past by editing it. It keeps the warm afternoons and discards the boredom, the injustice, the fear. This selective memory is harmless as private comfort but dangerous as politics, for a longing to return to a golden age that never quite existed has fueled some of history's worst decisions. The cure is not to forget the past, but to remember it whole.

questions.question: How does nostalgia treat the past?
options: Edits it, keeping only the good

questions.question: Why is it dangerous as politics?
options: It longs for a golden age that never existed
questions.explanation: 'a golden age that never quite existed'.

title: The Aesthetics of Imperfection (אסתטיקה של אי-שלמות)
text: Where Western design has often chased flawless symmetry, other traditions have prized the crack, the asymmetry, the trace of the maker's hand. There is a quiet wisdom in this: perfection, once attained, has nowhere left to go, while imperfection keeps a thing alive, unfinished, open to the eye that returns to it. The flaw is not a failure of beauty but a condition of it.

questions.question: What have some traditions prized?
How does the writer reframe the flaw?
questions.explanation: 'not a failure of beauty but a condition of it'.

title: The Map of Knowledge (מפת הידע)
text: The more one learns, the larger the perimeter of one's ignorance becomes. Each answer opens several new questions, so that the educated mind is, paradoxically, more aware of what it does not know than the novice who imagines the field to be small. Genuine expertise is thus accompanied not by certainty but by a refined sense of doubt.

questions.question: What grows as one learns more?
questions.explanation: 'the larger the perimeter of one's ignorance'.

questions.question: What accompanies genuine expertise?
questions.explanation: 'not by certainty but by a refined sense of doubt'.

title: Against Efficiency (נגד היעילות)
text: Efficiency is the unquestioned virtue of our age, but applied without limit it quietly devours the things that resist measurement. A perfectly efficient conversation is an interrogation; a perfectly efficient friendship is a transaction. Some of life's deepest goods — wandering, lingering, play — are precisely the ones that an efficiency mindset cannot help but classify as waste.

questions.question: What does limitless efficiency 'devour'?
How would an efficiency mindset classify wandering and play?

title: The Seduction of the Counterintuitive (פיתוי הבלתי-אינטואיטיבי)
text: There is a particular prestige attached to the counterintuitive claim — the finding that overturns common sense feels deeper, cleverer, more worth repeating. Yet common sense is often common because it is right, and an idea's surprise value is no measure of its truth. The contrarian who is reflexively contrarian is merely conventional in reverse.

questions.question: What feels 'deeper', per the text?

title: Translation and Loss (תרגום ואובדן)
text: To translate is to choose, repeatedly, what to sacrifice. A pun cannot survive intact in another tongue; a rhythm bends; a connotation evaporates. The finest translators are not those who lose nothing — that is impossible — but those who choose their losses with such care that the reader never feels the wound.

What marks the finest translators?
options: They choose their losses with care

title: The Comfort of Pessimism (נחמת הפסימיות)
text: Pessimism wears the costume of wisdom. To predict disaster is to risk nothing: if it comes, you were right; if it doesn't, you were merely prudent. Optimism, by contrast, is a wager that can be lost in public. Perhaps that is why gloom so often passes for depth, while hope is mistaken for naivety.

questions.question: Why is predicting disaster 'risk-free'?
options: Right if it comes, prudent if not
questions.explanation: 'if it comes, you were right; if it doesn't... prudent'.

questions.question: What is hope often mistaken for?

title: The Authenticity Trap (מלכודת האותנטיות)
text: We are urged endlessly to 'be authentic', as though the self were a fixed treasure to be uncovered rather than an ongoing act of creation. But the demand contains a paradox: the moment authenticity becomes a performance staged for others, it curdles into its opposite. Perhaps the most genuine people are those who never think to ask whether they are.

questions.question: How is 'be authentic' usually framed?
What paradox does the writer note?
options: As a performance, it becomes its opposite
questions.explanation: 'staged for others, it curdles into its opposite'.

title: The Limits of Empathy (גבולות האמפתיה)
text: Empathy is widely treated as an unalloyed good, but it has a quiet bias: it flows most easily toward the near, the visible, and the similar. The single named child moves us more than the statistic of thousands. A morality built on feeling alone will therefore be generous and unjust at once — vivid where it should be fair.

questions.question: What 'quiet bias' does empathy have?
options: Toward the near, visible and similar
questions.explanation: 'toward the near, the visible, and the similar'.

questions.question: What is the risk of a morality built on feeling alone?

title: The Vanity of Originality (יהירות המקוריות)
text: The modern artist is told, above all, to be original — yet originality pursued directly tends to curdle into mere novelty, a frantic search for the unsaid that mistakes strangeness for depth. The paradox is that the most enduring work often arises not from straining to differ, but from engaging so honestly with tradition that something genuinely new escapes, almost by accident.

questions.question: What does originality pursued directly tend to become?
Where does enduring work often arise from?

title: On Certainty (על הוודאות)
text: Certainty is psychologically comfortable and intellectually dangerous in almost equal measure. The mind craves a settled answer and will often manufacture one rather than endure the discomfort of suspension. But the willingness to hold a question open — to say 'I don't yet know' without flinching — may be the truest mark of a disciplined intelligence.

questions.question: How is certainty described?
What is called the mark of disciplined intelligence?
questions.explanation: 'the willingness to hold a question open'.
